hook: Simply naming what you're feeling — precisely — measurably reduces activity in the brain's threat response. Not fixing it. Just naming it.
topic: Affect labelling — the neuroscience of emotional naming
body:
**Researchers at UCLA used fMRI scanning to study what happens in the brain when you name an emotion.**

When people labelled their emotional state in precise language, activity in the amygdala — the brain's threat and alarm centre — measurably decreased. The prefrontal cortex, the rational, regulatory part of the brain, became more active. The labelling itself was the intervention.

But precision matters. "Stressed" and "anxious" are too broad. The effect is significantly stronger when the label is specific. Not "I feel bad." Something closer to: "I feel afraid that this situation is beyond my control." Or: "I feel ashamed that I didn't handle that better."

That specificity does something the vague label can't. It moves the experience from an undifferentiated threat signal into a categorised, comprehensible feeling — one the prefrontal cortex can actually work with.

You don't need to fix the feeling. You don't need to argue with it or replace it. You need to name it accurately.

That's the neurological lever. Precision over positivity.
